ageing_relevance.rationale: A large share of the papers concern ageing, and CST3 is linked to several age-related diseases and to the GrimAge mortality clock. Much of this reflects its use as a biomarker (kidney function, mortality), so causality is unproven.

evidence.value: One of seven plasma proteins whose DNA-methylation surrogates make up GrimAge

background_knowledge: Circulating cystatin C is a well-known marker of kidney function and predicts mortality and cardiovascular risk.
The GrimAge surrogate is a methylation estimate, not a measured protein level.

mechanism.rationale: CST3 is a secreted cysteine protease inhibitor with a known amyloidogenic variant (hereditary cerebral haemorrhage with amyloidosis). The direction for ageing is unclear: higher levels mark risk, but the protein may also be protective, for example against amyloid-β aggregation.

evidence.value: inhibitor of cysteine proteinases ... local regulator of this enzyme activity

background_knowledge: Cystatin C has been reported to be neuroprotective and to bind amyloid-β in Alzheimer disease models.
Plasma levels depend strongly on glomerular filtration rate, which confounds interpretation.

tractability.rationale: There is small-molecule evidence (structure with ligand, high-quality pocket) and antibody evidence because the protein is secreted. No approved modality exists and the protein has no obvious druggable activity.

safety.rationale: Open Targets lists no safety liabilities, but absence of data is not evidence of safety. Inhibiting a broad protease inhibitor could be harmful, and the protein is amyloidogenic in some variants.
background_knowledge: Cystatin C is widely expressed and acts as a general cysteine protease regulator, so unintended effects are plausible.

clinical_precedence.rationale: No drugs acting on CST3 have reached the clinic.

assessment.summary: CST3 (cystatin C) is a secreted cysteine protease inhibitor. It has good ageing relevance as a biomarker: about 25% of its papers mention ageing, it is associated with AMD, CKD and cardiovascular disease, and it is a GrimAge component. It is probably a marker more than a driver, and the direction of modulation is unclear because the protein may be protective in the brain. It has some small-molecule and antibody tractability, no clinical candidates and no listed safety liabilities, though that last point is only absence of data. I would consider it mainly as a biomarker or for mechanistic follow-up, not as a direct drug target.
key_uncertainties: Whether CST3 is causal for ageing or only a biomarker that tracks kidney function
Direction of modulation: raised levels mark risk, but the protein may be protective in neurodegeneration
The GrimAge surrogate is a DNA-methylation estimate, not measured protein
Safety data are absent, not shown to be benign
